content: Childhood obesity, also referred to as obesity in kids, obesity in children, or pediatric obesity, is defined as having a Body Mass Index (BMI) at or above the 95th percentile for children of the same age and gender. This condition is a significant health concern that can lead to various complications. The causes of childhood obesity include dietary habits, lifestyle factors, underlying medical conditions, genetic predispositions, or the use of certain medications. Children with obesity may present with symptoms such as high blood pressure, shortness of breath, sleep apnea, gastroesophageal reflux, constipation, insulin resistance, or irregular menstruation. The presence of excessive thirst (polydipsia) and frequent urination (polyuria) may indicate diabetes. Adolescent girls with insulin resistance, irregular menstruation, and excessive facial hair may have polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). Dry skin, constipation, and cold intolerance could suggest hypothyroidism. Laboratory tests are determined based on the clinical presentation. Management of childhood obesity involves addressing any underlying medical conditions and implementing lifestyle modifications. Treatment strategies include dietary changes, increased physical activity, and behavioral interventions. In some cases, bariatric surgery may be considered for adolescents with severe obesity. Preventive measures include exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months of life, consuming fruits and vegetables, drinking water, avoiding sugary snacks and beverages, engaging in regular physical activity, limiting screen time, reducing stress, and maintaining a healthy sleep routine. Historically, obesity was first recognized as a medical disorder by Hippocrates, the ancient Greek physician. In the 11th century, Avicenna described complications of obesity, such as narrowed blood vessels, stroke, and breathing difficulties, in his medical text The Canon of Medicine. Childhood obesity can be classified based on ageand gender-adjusted BMI into two categories: obesity (BMI ≥ 95th percentile) and severe obesity (BMI ≥ 120% of the 95th percentile or BMI ≥ 35 kg/m²). The pathophysiology of childhood obesity involves fat accumulation due to an energy imbalance, which results from excessive calorie intake and/or reduced calorie expenditure. Dysregulation of the ghrelin/leptin hormonal pathway may contribute to abnormal appetite control and energy balance. Genetic mutations in single genes, such as leptin (LEP), leptin receptor (LEPR), and pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC), have been linked to some cases of childhood obesity. The causes of childhood obesity are multifactorial. Dietary factors include the consumption of low-nutrient, high-calorie foods and beverages, such as fast food and sugar-sweetened drinks. Lifestyle factors, such as physical inactivity, excessive screen time, and inadequate sleep, also play a role. Environmental factors, including school lunch policies, parental work demands, and demographics, influence eating habits. Chronic psychological stress increases the risk of obesity, diabetes, heart disease, metabolic syndrome, and mental health issues. Endocrine disorders, such as hypothyroidism, Cushing's syndrome, PCOS, precocious puberty, and pseudohypoparathyroidism, may also contribute to weight gain. Genetic causes include monogenic obesity (e.g., mutations in LEP, LEPR, POMC, MC4R, PC1/2, SIM1, NTRK2/BDNF, and SH2B1), syndromic obesity (e.g., Prader-Willi syndrome, Cohen syndrome, Turner syndrome, Down syndrome, and Laurence-Moon-Bardet-Biedl syndrome), and polygenic obesity. Certain medications, such as second-generation antipsychotics, glucocorticoids, risperidone, clozapine, and tricyclic antidepressants, can induce weight gain. Cerebral injuries, such as hypothalamic lesions following surgery, meningitis, or ischemic injury, may also lead to obesity. Differentiating childhood obesity due to lifestyle factors from other diseases is essential. Conditions such as hypothyroidism, Cushing's syndrome, and PCOS must be ruled out. The global prevalence of childhood obesity is significant, with approximately 38 million children under the age of 5 affected in 2019 and over 340 million children aged 5 to 19 affected in 2016. In the United States, childhood obesity is more common among adolescents aged 12 to 19 years, followed by children aged 6 to 11 years, and then those aged 2 to 5 years. Males are more commonly affected than females in many highand upper-middle-income countries. Racial disparities exist, with higher obesity prevalence among Hispanic and non-Hispanic Black children compared to non-Hispanic White and non-Hispanic Asian children. Common risk factors for childhood obesity include a high-calorie diet, lack of physical activity, having obese family members, stress, and living in low-income households. If left untreated, childhood obesity can lead to complications such as glucose intolerance, type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, asthma, obstructive sleep apnea, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, gallstones, joint pain, and depression. Obese children are at increased risk of progressing to adult obesity and developing heart disease, diabetes, and certain cancers. They often face weight stigma, teasing, bullying, and discrimination, which can result in low self-esteem, anxiety, and depression. The diagnosis of childhood obesity in children aged 2 and older is made when the BMI is at or above the 95th percentile on the BMI-for-age growth chart. Symptoms may include shortness of breath, sleep apnea, constipation, gastroesophageal reflux, and irregular menstruation. Physical examination findings may include stretch marks on the hips and abdomen, acanthosis nigricans, and signs of hypothyroidism (e.g., dry skin, constipation, and fatigue). Features such as fat accumulation in the neck and trunk, moon facies, facial plethora, acne, and hirsutism may suggest Cushing's syndrome. Early sexual development may indicate precocious puberty, while acne, hirsutism, and acanthosis nigricans in adolescent girls may suggest PCOS. Laboratory tests for overweight and obese children include hemoglobin A1C, fasting plasma glucose, 2-hour plasma glucose, and fasting lipids. Additional tests may be indicated based on clinical presentation, such as thyroid function tests (TSH, T4, T3, free T4), adrenal function tests, liver function tests, serum leptin, serum calcium, phosphorus, parathyroid hormone, gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist stimulation test, and measurements of free testosterone, total testosterone, LH, FSH, and dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate. The primary goal of treatment is to safely reduce BMI, prevent complications, and manage existing comorbidities. Lifestyle modification through diet, exercise, and behavioral changes is the cornerstone of therapy. In some cases, medications approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) may be used for children aged 6 and older with obesity caused by rare genetic disorders. Bariatric surgery may be considered for adolescents with severe obesity. Prevention strategies include promoting healthy eating habits, regular physical activity, limiting screen time, reducing stress, and ensuring adequate sleep.
